summary:
Consensual sex between adult men is a criminal offence under Article 135 of the Criminal Code. The maximum sentence is two years' imprisonment, with a further two to five years in a labour camp possible under some readings of the provision. Article 19 permits increased penalties for repeat convictions. A 2019 amendment raised the maximum above the two-year ceiling set in 1997, and ILGA-Europe's 2025 annual review records that the Criminal Code adopted in April 2022 retained the sodomy provisions while increasing both the severity and the scope of the punishments attached to them.

Trans people are an unacknowledged category in Turkmen law. No provision addresses gender recognition and no legal mechanism exists to change identity documents. The same silence covers women who have relationships with women, for whom no penal provision exists. The practical exposure for a trans visitor turns on how the authorities read their birth-sex status: a trans woman whose identity documents record a male sex, or a trans man in a relationship the authorities would read as between two men, falls within the scope of Article 135.

There is no anti-discrimination legislation. The government has rejected requests to adopt one made through three Universal Periodic Reviews, and in February 2021 told the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights that it intended to 'study the option of introducing anti-discrimination legislation'. In UN human rights dialogue it has justified its framework by arguing that any deviation poses a potential threat to the fabric of Turkmen traditions and society.

Enforcement of Article 135 was rare before Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow became president in 2006. Reported consequences since then include state-sponsored violence and torture during criminal investigation, interrogation that witnesses describe as grossly humiliating, and vigilante attacks that are especially common in prison. ILGA-Europe reports that torture and inhuman treatment remain present throughout the country, with relatives reporting LGBTI people among those subjected to them. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report on Turkmenistan lists laws criminalising consensual same-sex conduct between adults among the country's significant human rights issues, alongside officials in the security services committing abuses and engaging in corruption with impunity.

Suspects in Article 135 cases face interrogation, torture and confinement to mental hospitals. In October 2019 a gay doctor was tortured by the state apparatus over a prolonged period before temporarily disappearing. In May 2020 several well-known figures from the modelling industry were arrested on charges of homosexuality.

The persecution documented in asylum proceedings is a measure of what people flee. In 2007 a US law clinic secured asylum for a Turkmen woman persecuted for being a lesbian and for her political opinions, believed to be the first such grant for a lesbian from Turkmenistan. In 2019 attorneys secured asylum for a lesbian couple from Turkmenistan who feared imprisonment and torture.

A 2020 civil-society submission to the UN human rights review process concluded that LGBT people in Turkmenistan have no effective legislative means of enjoying their fundamental human rights, and identified Article 135 as the core foundation of profound systemic discrimination.
tangentialFactors:
Turkmenistan is one of only two post-Soviet states where sex between men remains a criminal offence, the other being Uzbekistan.

The framework has been raised repeatedly in UN human rights mechanisms, including three Universal Periodic Review cycles and correspondence with the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights.
localsOnly:
Repeat convictions can lead to compulsory psychiatric admission and involuntary conversion therapy. Within those facilities homosexuality is institutionally perceived as a form of mental disorder.

Women who come to official attention are vulnerable to sexual violence and to killings framed as matters of family honour.

The 2020 civil-society submission records increasing flight abroad as the practical response for those at risk, and groups people living with HIV with LGBT people as lacking effective legislative means of enjoying their fundamental human rights.
outOfScopeNotes:
The precise penalty structure of the April 2022 Criminal Code is not set out in the available sources; the increase in severity and scope is reported without the amended text.

Whether the February 2021 stated intention to study anti-discrimination legislation produced a draft or any legislative step is not sourced.

Data on these issues is scarce: the media is entirely state-owned and no civil society organisations operate in the country, so incident counts and enforcement frequency are not independently verifiable.

No trans-specific healthcare access findings, and no youth- or minor-specific care access findings, appear in the sources reviewed.

No gender-recognition procedure is documented in the sources. The absence of a legal category for trans people is reported, but administrative practice at entry, in screening or in detention is not documented.
